identification.name: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma Stotram (one verse)
identification.source: Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, Uttara-khaṇḍa, Lalitopākhyāna (Hayagrīva–Agastya dialogue); Lalitā Sahasranāma stotra, approx. verse 49
identification.notes: The text of the verse is the standard reading of the Lalitā Sahasranāma. The exact verse number varies between editions, depending on whether the pūrva-bhāga verses are counted; verse 49 is the common numbering of the stotra proper. The ten names (Nirlepā … Nirupaplavā) belong to the series of 'nir-' names describing the nirguṇa aspect of the Devī.

meaning_summary: This verse of the Lalitā Sahasranāma praises the Devī in her transcendent, attribute-less aspect. She is untouched by anything, stainless, eternal, formless and untroubled. She is beyond the guṇas and without parts. She is peace itself, free of desire, and free from every calamity or disturbance.

story.speaker: Hayagrīva
story.frame: The Lalitā Sahasranāma is taught by Hayagrīva (a form of Viṣṇu) to the sage Agastya in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
story.legend: According to the frame of the text, the thousand names were composed by the Vāgdevīs (the speech-goddesses Vaśinī and the others) at the command of Lalitā herself. They recited the names before her assembled court, and she declared this hymn especially dear to her. Hayagrīva later reveals it to Agastya, who had asked for this secret hymn.
story.setting: Dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya; the original recitation takes place in Lalitā's court
story.source: Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, Uttara-khaṇḍa, Lalitopākhyāna (Lalitā Sahasranāma pūrva-bhāga and uttara-bhāga)

lines.english: She who is untainted, stainless and eternal,

words.meaning: untainted, untouched by anything (e.g. by karma or attachment)
unperturbed, free from agitation or confusion

lines.english: beyond the guṇas, without parts, peaceful,
desireless and free from all calamity or disturbance.

words.meaning: free from affliction, calamity or destruction; imperishable

caution: Verse numbering differs between editions, so check it against the book your group uses. Commentators such as Bhāskararāya give layered interpretations of these names; for example, 'nirupaplavā' is variously explained as 'free from calamity', 'imperishable', or 'free from the disturbance of the senses'. The glosses given here are the plain meanings. The story attribution follows the Purāṇic frame of the Sahasranāma as a whole and is not specific to this verse.
